messages.subject_clean: Spatial Capture-Recapture Workshop, 12-14 March 2018, Banff, Canada
messages.body_plain:
Spatial Capture-Recapture Workshop in Banff

Instructors
Andy Royle (USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center)
Richard Chandler (University of Georgia)
Angela Fuller (USGS and Cornell University)

Date: 12-14 March 2018 (3 days)

Location: Banff, Canada

Cost
USD$600 (normal rate) or USD$450 (student rate). Cost includes
breakfast, lunch, and refreshment breaks.

Overview
This course introduces key models used in the analysis of
spatially-explicit capture-recapture data using Bayesian and classical
(likelihood) methods. It closely follows material from the book
"Spatial Capture-Recapture" (Elsevier, 2014). The workshop will cover
basic model and data analysis concepts in R and the BUGS language
(using WinBUGS or JAGS), analysis of classical capture-recapture
models (models M0, Mb, Mh, etc...), concepts and methods of spatial
capture-recapture models and their analysis using the R package "oSCR"
and also using the BUGS language. Advanced topics will include open
population models and integrated population models.

Registration
Registration information and additional information about the workshop
can be found here: http://conted.warnell.uga.edu/courses/cap-recap2018

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jesse,

It could be that the species 2 is really underdetected so much (and the estimate of p of 0.13 seems to suggest so), but in addition, site-occupancy models are also known to produce biased estimates of psi and p when p is low, where “low” typically means something in the region of 0.2 or below. See the simulation results in the original occupancy paper 2002. If you have access to the book Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology (Kéry & Royle, 2016), we also say this and demonstrate it using a simulation in chapter 10.

Best regards  --Marc

This is definitely an issue with maximum likelihood estimate for these problems:  when the true detection probability is low, there is a tendency for the maximum likelihood estimate to be 1.0 for psi.  As support that occu is doing everything correctly consider the log of the likelihood surface:

The red dot shows the maximum likelihood estimates for psi and p.

Going Bayesian is a step forward but it's not just about the posterior means:  the posterior variance and the shape of the posterior distribution needs to be taken into account.  Here are the marginal posterior distributions of psi and p when the prior is a uniform distribution:
​

So one can't rule out a value near 1.0 for psi even if one is a Bayesian.

Hi everyone,

Hopefully this isn't a redundant topic but I haven't been able to find a previous thread that addresses it. I am using dynamic n-mixture models to estimate tadpole density and survival over the course of the summer. Because there shouldn't be any recruitment over my trapping period, I fixed the gamma parameter:

am5 <- pcountOpen(~WetlandType+ElevationM+Year, ~1, ~1, ~offset(log(numTraps)) , AmtiAbundUmf, K=50,fix= "gamma", mixture="ZIP")

When I try to evaluate goodness of fit using the Nmix.gof.test or parboot functions I get the error:

Nmix.gof.test(am5, nsim = 50)
"Error in Xgam %*% coef(object, "gamma") : requires numeric/complex matrix/vector arguments"

Does anyone know of a way to get around this problem? These functions work just fine when I allow gamma to be estimated.

If not, any thoughts on whether I can evaluate goodness of fit with gamma in the model?

Thank you!

messages.subject_clean: pcount: Low detection probabilities for common species
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kate,

The N-mixture model fit using the function pcount assumes closure--in other words, N (the number of birds at a site) is treated as having a specific and fixed value over the duration of the survey. This assumption is almost definitely not true over three years of sampling, and maybe not true across even a single season (bird movement induces heterogeneity in # birds available for detection, i.e., N at a specific time may vary).  Ignoring this heterogeneity will certainly bias p and lambda, and I'd guess your estimates are further wonky because of the null model structure (i.e., p and and N are likely to vary spatially regardless of the temporal sampling nature). The Applied Hierarchical Modeling book (v1, Kery and Royle) touches on this in greater detail.  You might look into pcountopen (aka Dail-Madsen models) or gpcount (no informal model name, but following Chandler et al. 2011 regarding temporary emigration) as alternatives.

--John
